title: Wings over his brother
hookLine: two young brothers race toward the sun

cards: Two brothers race straight up toward the sun. It's day six hundred, and Sampati is telling the monkeys how it began. When Jatayu and I were young, he says, we were proud of our flying.
We were rivals the way brothers are, each sure he was the stronger. So one day we raced. It's an old kind of contest: two brothers, each needing to win, neither willing to turn back first.

teach.b: They climbed until the earth below looked small. Then the heat came.

Jatayu, the younger, began to faint, and Sampati spread his own wings over his brother to shade him. His wings burned. He fell, landed here on the Vindhya hills, and has lived without wings ever since.
Many teachers read that race as ahankara, the Hindu word for ego, literally the I-maker: the part of you that has to be the biggest, the fastest, the first.
The Bhagavad Gita lists it among the things a wise person lets go of. Notice what ahankara did: it sent two brothers straight at the sun. And notice what the story remembers.
Not who flew higher, but the moment Sampati stopped racing and covered his brother. The race was for the I; the burn was for love. Then he waited, a long time.
A sage named Nishakara comforted him and told him that one day Rama's messengers would come searching for Sita, and if Sampati helped them, his wings would grow back.
Without wings he couldn't hunt, so his son Suparshva brought him food. One day Suparshva came back late and empty-handed. He had seen a dark giant flying over the sea carrying a weeping woman.
That was Ravana, Sampati tells the monkeys. That was your Sita. And the monkeys, who sat down to die an hour ago, sit up straight.

how: Storytellers often pair Sampati's sacrifice for Jatayu with Jatayu's sacrifice for Sita: two brothers, each burned or wounded for someone else.

games.q: you're Sampati, flying at the sun beside your younger brother. he starts to faint in the heat. what do you do?
o: spread your wings over him to shade him.
games.why: Sampati shades Jatayu with his own wings; they burn, and he falls to the Vindhya hills.

practice: Let your arms rest open a little, like folded wings. Think of somewhere you're racing someone right now: for a grade, for credit, for the last word. Breathe in and notice the I that needs to win; Hindus call it ahankara.
Breathe out and picture spreading a wing over the person you're racing instead. You don't have to lose. Just notice which moment you'd want remembered.

wordCard.voice: Sampati. He lost his wings shading his brother from the sun, and waited, wingless, for Rama's messengers.

orig.note: Sanskrit pakṣa: a wing; also a side, or a party one takes sides with.

carryVoice: Your line: ahankara races, love shields. Six hundred days of showing up. See you tomorrow.
